summary:
Karnātaka stands under India's national framework for transgender recognition and protection. The operative baseline for a trans visitor is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill passed by both houses of India's Parliament in March 2026, which narrows the 2019 Act it amends.

The amendment removes the self-identification route to legal recognition established under the 2019 law and reverses the recognition principle set by the Supreme Court in 2014. Recognition is now restricted to persons belonging to traditionally or historically recognised socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex persons. Self-identified trans men, trans women and non-binary people who fall outside those categories are outside the recognition scheme.

Recognition also requires medical certification. Under the amended law, medical boards and district authorities certify whether gender-affirming surgery has been performed, replacing a self-declaration process with an administrative and medical determination of identity.

The amendment adds offences, including a crime carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warned on 26 March 2026 that this provision could be used against support networks and allies of trans people rather than against their exploiters.

Recognition coverage in practice is narrow. The census records 487,803 transgender persons in India, of whom approximately 32,500 hold identity cards. Government estimates put the transgender population at around two million, a figure well above the census count.

Parliament passed the bill in March 2026 and presidential assent was still pending as of late March 2026, with Human Rights Watch urging the president not to sign it. A Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, describing the removal of self-identification as a setback to the 2014 ruling. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics state that it excludes many trans men, trans women and non-binary people.

No Karnātaka-specific enforcement series or incident pattern was identified in the country-level research, so this state is assessed at the national score. A visitor in Karnātaka operates under the same narrowed recognition regime, medical certification requirement and checkpoint exposure as elsewhere in India.
tangentialFactors:
Entry and stay rest on a mixed record. The Supreme Court decriminalised same-sex acts in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have read to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are unavailable, though courts have recognised same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024, when the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code and removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded transgender people from sexual violence. Trans communities report fear of increased assaults under the new code.

Document and checkpoint friction is the main exposure point. A trans woman alleged groping by a Railway Protection Force constable at a Kolkata railway station during a gender check; transgender detainees described degrading treatment by the Railway Protection Force in Assam in interviews recorded in June 2024; and Central Industrial Security Force personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024 despite her PAN card. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to undergo a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

High courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issued guidelines on police sensitisation, banned conversion therapy and directed the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, more likely in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing consequences of the March 2026 amendment concentrate on identity documents and welfare access. Only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender persons hold identity cards, and under the amended scheme obtaining or renewing such a card depends on medical boards and district authorities rather than self-declaration.

Access to welfare schemes and anti-trafficking protection is tied to the narrowed definition of who counts as transgender, which the government states is the purpose of the restriction. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people outside the hijra, kinner and intersex categories are excluded from that definition and, with it, from scheme eligibility.

Support networks face a distinct exposure: the new offence covering coercion or alluring a person to be transgender carries up to life imprisonment, and Human Rights Watch states it could be applied to those who assist trans people rather than to traffickers.

Transgender rights activists in India, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. Domestic litigation and political pressure remain active, including the Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel's request that the government withdraw the bill.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill was pending as of late March 2026; whether it has since been assented to, challenged or enjoined is unresolved in the sources available here.

No Karnātaka-specific court decisions, police practice records or incident series were sourced for this state, so the enforcement picture here is carried from national and other-state evidence rather than local documentation.

The census count of 487,803 transgender persons and the estimated population of around two million diverge substantially; the sources do not reconcile the two figures.

Whether the 2024 removal of gender-identity-specific offences from the penal code has produced a measurable rise in assaults is reported as a community fear, not as a documented increase in the sources cited.
